title: How OpenAI runs untrusted agent code in microVMs
subtitle: The sandbox cloud behind ChatGPT and Codex web: hardware-isolated microVMs, block-level snapshots, smart placement.
hook: Snapshots return before the upload ends and ship only changed disk blocks, so agents can checkpoint often.

sources.title: From fork() to Fleet: Designing an Agent Sandbox Cloud
sources.speaker: Abhishek Bhardwaj

nodes.label: Model
nodes.detail: Trained to call code execution on problems with checkable answers, like counting letters in a word, instead of guessing from memory.
nodes.tradeoff: Research needs throughput across many rollouts; the product needs low latency, or users churn.

nodes.label: Agent harness
nodes.detail: Parses the model's reply, and when it says to execute code, calls the tool somewhere: a laptop for local agents, a cloud node for ChatGPT and Codex web.
nodes.tradeoff: Even a well-meaning model may try to get root to help you, so the code is treated as untrusted.

nodes.label: Control plane
nodes.detail: Nodes are grouped into clusters spread across regions. The top-level control plane picks a cluster by region, load and other factors, ideally near the ChatGPT cluster.
nodes.tradeoff: Low latency and reliability stay the north stars for every placement decision.

nodes.label: Node scheduler
nodes.detail: Inside a cluster it picks a node by load and skips failing ones. On a restore it scores highest the node that already holds the snapshot's layers.
nodes.tradeoff: Snapshot-aware routing means less to download, so creates are faster and more reliable.

nodes.label: Warm pool
nodes.detail: Keeps pre-warmed sandboxes ready, or starts a microVM just in time from a saved memory snapshot in milliseconds. A hybrid grows the pool from that snapshot.
nodes.tradeoff: A warm pool burns CPU and memory while idle; memory snapshots avoid that cost.

nodes.label: MicroVM
nodes.detail: A Rust VMM process is created with a kernel, root file system, CPU and memory, then started on /dev/kvm. Root inside the guest still has no control of the host.
nodes.tradeoff: Every guest exit costs performance, memory is reclaimed slowly, and a VFIO GPU serves one sandbox at a time.

nodes.label: Guest API server
nodes.detail: PID 1 inside the guest exposes an API server. The harness reaches it over vsock to run commands, save state or attach devices.
nodes.tradeoff: Inside is a whole Linux box, and models drive Linux well because they were pre-trained on so much of it.

nodes.label: Block cache
nodes.detail: The guest sees a normal block device. Writes go to an in-cluster cache, which writes back to durable object storage.
nodes.tradeoff: NFS was rejected as slower and not POSIX-compliant, and models work best with standard POSIX.

nodes.label: Snapshot store
nodes.detail: A save call finds changed blocks on a copy-on-write layer, zips the diff, uploads it and returns a snapshot ID. Restore replays the layer lineage onto the base image.
nodes.tradeoff: Saving gigabytes every turn would bankrupt the company, so only the diff between snapshots is stored.

flow.text: Writes code to count letters instead of guessing the answer.
Parses the reply and requests a sandbox to run the code.
Picks a cluster near ChatGPT, weighing region and load.
Picks the healthy node that already holds the most snapshot layers.
Starts the microVM in milliseconds from a saved memory snapshot.
Cloud Hypervisor runs the guest on KVM, walled off by hardware.
The guest's PID 1 API runs the code and returns the result.
Changed blocks are zipped and uploaded; a snapshot ID returns right away.

takeaways.text: Containers and gVisor still sit on the host kernel, so a chained exploit can reach it.
Teams try containers, gVisor and V8 first, then end up wanting a VM: start with microVMs.
Storage is the next unlock: fast snapshot and restore let harnesses recover from failures and explore.
